desc:
A border of a string s is a non-empty proper prefix of s that is also a suffix of s. Return the lengths of all borders of s in increasing order. If s has no border, return an empty array.

Example: s = "abaabaaba" has the borders "a", "aba" and "abaaba", so the answer is [1,3,6].
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Comparing every prefix length with the same-length suffix is O(n<sup>2</sup>). Do you really need to examine every length?
The longest border can be read from the prefix function: it is pi[n-1].
Every shorter border of s is also a border of the longest border. So walk the chain k = pi[n-1], then pi[k-1], then pi[pi[k-1]-1], ... until it reaches zero, and reverse the collected lengths.
editorial: Compute the prefix function of s. The longest border has length b = pi[n-1]. A shorter border c is both a prefix and a suffix of s; since it is a prefix of the longest border and also a suffix of it (it sits at the end of s, inside the final b characters), c is a border of s[0..b-1] as well. Its longest such border has length pi[b-1], and so on.
So the full list of borders is the chain b, pi[b-1], pi[pi[b-1]-1], ... until the value hits 0. Collect it and reverse it to get increasing order.
Building pi costs O(n); the chain has at most n links. Total O(n) time. The Z-function gives an alternative: position i starts a border exactly when i + z[i] == n, and its length is n - i.
solution:
def allBorders(s):
    n = len(s)
    pi = [0] * n
    k = 0
    for i in range(1, n):
        while k and s[i] != s[k]:
            k = pi[k - 1]
        if s[i] == s[k]:
            k += 1
        pi[i] = k
    res = []
    k = pi[-1]
    while k:
        res.append(k)
        k = pi[k - 1]
    res.reverse()
    return res
